The Savanna path shrew Crocidura viaria, like many small-bodied soricids, likely exhibits a relatively high mass-specific metabolic rate. Limited data from congeners suggest that the resting metabolic rate measured in a thermoneutral zone approximates 22.1 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 22.1 milliliters of oxygen per hour] under standard laboratory conditions at 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C]. This elevated oxygen consumption reflects the high energetic demands associated with maintaining endothermy in a diminutive body and supports a life history characterized by rapid growth and early reproduction. Available records indicate that neonates weigh a mere 0.95 grams [Wwb = 0.95 grams], a value typical of the altricial young produced by crocidurine shrews, which are born in a highly undeveloped state following a short gestation period. This minimal birth mass underscores the substantial maternal investment required for successful embryonic and postnatal development.

Comparative data from the closely related Crocidura russula provide a useful proxy for certain life history traits of C. viaria when direct empirical measurements are unavailable. For instance, the gestation time for this species is estimated at 29 days [tg = 29 days], a duration that is consistent among small shrews when maintained at a body temperature of 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C]. This relatively brief intrauterine period is followed by a phase of intensive lactation during which the suckling juvenile gains mass rapidly. Field observations suggest that the wet weight at weaning, a critical developmental milestone marking nutritional independence, is approximately 7.8 grams [Wwx = approximately 7.8 grams]. This value, again derived from Crocidura russula, indicates that offspring more than octuple their birth mass before transitioning to a fully insectivorous diet.

The developmental trajectory of this species is tightly compressed. Based on the life history schedule of related crocidurines, the time since birth at weaning is estimated to be 23 days [tx = 23 days] under typical conditions at 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C]. The post-weaning juvenile period is likewise brief, with the attainment of puberty occurring approximately 75 days after birth [tp = approximately 75 days after birth] at the same ambient temperature. This remarkably accelerated maturation allows young shrews to enter the breeding population within their first season, a strategy common in small mammals facing high extrinsic mortality rates. Consequently, individuals can achieve multiple reproductive events within a single calendar year, maximizing lifetime fitness in a stochastic environment.

Reproduction in the Savanna path shrew is characterized by high fecundity relative to body size. Females typically produce litters of four pups per litter [N_R_i = four pups per litter], and under favorable conditions they may complete as many as three and a half litters per year [F_R_i = three and a half litters per year]. This intense annual reproductive output is consistent with the pattern observed in many small-bodied Crocidura species and is facilitated by the extremely brief gestation and rapid post-natal development described above. This lifespan balances a high reproductive rate against the energetic costs of sustained metabolic activity.

The ultimate wet weight achieved by adult Savanna path shrews, representing the asymptotic body mass after the cessation of growth, is approximately 14.7 grams [Wwi = approximately 14.7 grams]. This modest adult size places C. viaria in the middle of the size range for its genus. Integrating these demographic parameters, the species exemplifies a classic fast life history strategy, with high daily reproductive output, early maturation, and short lifespan all facilitated by a high basal metabolic rate. The physiological underpinnings of this strategy are evident in the oxygen consumption data, which reveal the substantial energetic infrastructure required to sustain such a rapid pace of life. Future field studies should focus on directly validating these inferred measurements in wild populations across the species’ range.
